title: Delaware Winter Camps on Kentucky Ground
summary: Lenape (Delaware) bands—often alongside Shawnee, Mingo, Miami, and Wyandot—used Kentucky as seasonal hunting country rather than a place of large permanent towns, after…
bodyMarkdown:
Lenape (Delaware) bands—often alongside Shawnee, Mingo, Miami, and Wyandot—used Kentucky as seasonal hunting country rather than a place of large permanent towns, after colonial land pressure, including Pennsylvania’s 1737 Walking Purchase, pushed Lenape people west into Ohio. From villages north of the Ohio they slipped south in fall and winter for deer and bear, leaving small camps that Anglo hunters mistook for emptiness, though none of the sources cited here documents a specific Delaware camp site in Kentucky. By the 1770s those same parties faced settler pressure and increasingly turned from hunts into raids. The “dark and bloody ground” myth grew from that pattern: real Native use, but not the empty wilderness Filson’s readers imagined.
Source: [A. Gwynn Henderson, “Dispelling the Myth: Seventeenth- and Eighteenth-Century Indian Life in Kentucky,” Register of the Kentucky Historical Society 90, no. 1 (1992) (PDF)](https://preservationkentucky.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Dispelling-the-Myth-17th-18th-Century-Indian-Life-in-KY.pdf)
Source: [History (Delaware Nation, Anadarko, Oklahoma)](https://www.delawarenation-nsn.gov/history/)
